newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices steady despite comfortable U.S. stocks.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices steady despite comfortable U.S. stocks.

text.p: World oil prices fell then recovered on Thursday after the latest energy data from the United States showed the world's biggest consumer was well stocked with crude oil and oil products last week.
World marker crude Brent Blend from the North Sea for July delivery traded down to a low of $19.10 a barrel before bouncing back to trade one cent up at $19.25 in the London afternoon.
Brent crude tumbled by 78 cents on Tuesday when investment funds joined a sell-off sparked by fears the market was brimming with long positions.

"Overall there is still quite a quantity of fund money in the market, probably around current levels, and prices could ultimately rally again if they are not shaken out," brokers GNI said in a daily market report.

Two sets of data from the United States on Wednesday and Thursday showed that crude oil stocks rose last week largely because of increased imports. Stocks of distillates -- which include heating oil -- were also higher.
But the separate reports by the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) differed over gasoline, which is crucial to price direction at this time of year.
The DOE report showed gasoline inventories rose 1.1 million barrels while the API figures indicated a decline of 1.1 million barrels.
Despite the discrepancies, traders said the inventory data this week was within the range of expectations and likely to have already been priced into the market.

"Demand is pretty good in gasoline, but with (refinery) operations up near 97 percent it all looks neutral. Supply and demand seem to be very much in balance," said Thomas Blakeslee, analyst at Cargill Investor services in New York.

Brent crude had rallied $1 a barrel in the two weeks before Tuesday as U.S. refineries ratcheted up gasoline production in preparation for the unofficial start of the peak summer driving season, traditionally marked by Monday's Memorial Day holiday.
But dealers are divided on whether U.S. gasoline can sustain oil prices at levels still running nearly $3 higher on average this year than in the four years from 1991-1995 after the Gulf War.
